title: Advantages and disadvantages of union activity

blocks.heading: What this section covers
blocks.text: Identify the factors that influence the strength of a trade union, weigh the advantages and disadvantages of trade union activity for workers, firms, the government and the economy, and state what the outcome depends on.
blocks.repair_note: coverage gaps filled from syllabus guidance

blocks.heading: What unions can achieve
blocks.text: For workers the advantage is direct: a negotiated rise lifts pay, and negotiated rules make the workplace safer and treatment more predictable. For the firm there can be an offsetting gain: workers who feel fairly dealt with tend to stay, so the firm recruits and trains fewer replacements, and a settled relationship with the union loses fewer days to disputes. For the economy, unions bargaining for low-paid workers tend to narrow the gap between low and higher pay, and the income they win is spent in local shops - traders near the Oshakati textile plant see it each pay day.

blocks.heading: Where the costs land
blocks.text: The costs are just as real. A wage rise won in bargaining raises the firm's pay bill hour by hour: at Marula Meat Processors, an abattoir in Gobabis, a deal lifting the rate from N$10.00 to N$11.00 an hour added N$1.00 for every hour its 180 union members work. A firm facing dearer labour may raise prices, and where its buyers can switch to cheaper imports it may instead let its workforce shrink by not replacing workers who leave. Industrial action is the sharpest cost: a three-day stoppage at the abattoir lost N$96 000 of output, and the striking workers lost three days' pay. Dock unions at the port of Rotterdam in the Netherlands know the same arithmetic.

blocks.heading: What makes a union strong
blocks.text: A union's strength is its power to win what it bargains for, and several conditions shape it. Membership: a union that has signed up 90% of a workforce can halt production; one with 20% may barely be noticed. Skills: members who are hard to replace, such as qualified electricians at a mine, carry more weight than workers an employer can hire and train in a day. The state of the economy: when unemployment is low, employers struggle to find replacements, while in a slump the fear of losing a job weakens the union. The employer's position: a profitable firm with strong demand for its product can afford a rise more readily. The law: rules that protect the right to strike strengthen a union, and rules that restrict it weaken one. Funds: a union with savings can support members through a strike. Public support: a union whose cause the public backs puts more pressure on the employer and the government.

blocks.heading: The government's view
blocks.text: The government sees union activity from a third side. It can gain: unions give it one body to consult when it drafts labour law, disputes settled at a bargaining table cost less than strikes, pay rises for low-paid workers can narrow the gap between rich and poor and reduce the need for state support, and higher wages bring in more income tax. It can lose: a strike by nurses, teachers or bus drivers stops public services the government is responsible for; as an employer itself, the government faces union pay claims that add to its budget; pay rises that outpace output can push up prices; and where higher labour costs lead firms to cut jobs or invest in other countries, lost jobs and lost tax follow. Which side weighs more tends to depend on whether bargaining stays at the table and whether pay rises are matched by output.

blocks.heading: What the balance depends on
blocks.text: Whether union activity helps or harms depends on three conditions. Whether the pay rise matches output per worker: where it does, the firm can pay the rise out of extra production; where it does not, costs rise with no extra income to cover them. Whether the economy is creating jobs: in a growing economy a firm can carry higher pay and keep hiring; in a weak one it sheds them. And whether the union and the employer bargain or fight: a settlement reached at a table costs both sides less than one reached on a picket line.
